overview: The 7805 (fixed 5V output, TO-220 package) and AMS1117 (fixed 3.3V is common, small SOT-223 package) are linear regulators — the simplest possible way to get a clean, stable voltage from a higher, less-stable input: just three pins, no switching, no inductor. The tradeoff for that simplicity is heat: a linear regulator burns off the entire input-to-output voltage difference as heat proportional to current draw, so regulating 12V down to 5V at any real current gets the small metal tab genuinely hot — a buck converter does the same job far more efficiently, but with more components and complexity.
simpleSummary: A simple 3-pin part that turns a rough input voltage into a clean, steady one, like 5V or 3.3V.

specifications.dropoutVoltage: ~2V (7805, needs input at least 2V above output); ~1.1V (AMS1117 low-dropout)
specifications.package: TO-220 (7805, with metal tab for heatsinking), SOT-223 (AMS1117)

pinMap.name: IN
pinMap.currentLimit: Depends on load and required output current
pinMap.gotcha: Input must exceed the output voltage by at least the dropout voltage, or the output sags below its rated value.

pinMap.name: GND
pinMap.function: Ground reference, shared between input and output.

pinMap.name: OUT
pinMap.gotcha: At real currents, the voltage difference times the current becomes heat — a 7805 dropping 12V to 5V at 500mA dissipates 3.5W, hot enough to need a heatsink.

useCases.title: Simple fixed-voltage power supply
useCases.scenario: Generate a clean 5V or 3.3V rail from a higher unregulated battery or wall-adapter voltage for low-current logic circuits.

useCases.title: Breadboard power supply module
useCases.scenario: The classic beginner breadboard power supply board is usually built around one of these chips.

oftenConfusedWith: LM2596 buck converter (switching, far more efficient at higher currents, needs more components)
oftenUpgradedTo: LM2596 or similar switching regulator once heat/efficiency becomes a real concern
